genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the main figure looks after the animals at a shelter
she walks into the enclosure before the sky lightens
she likens her work to that of an interpreter
a thick-furred mammal states its needs differently from a bird
she raises motherless newborns on a bottle
she keeps her distance when a grown animal is hurt
she compares her patience to that of someone tending a plot of ground
her colleagues credit her with sensing pain before any visible sign
she puts that reputation down to close and repeated watching
text: The keeper crosses the enclosure before the sky begins to lighten, a bucket of feed braced against her hip. Her work, she likes to say, is closer to an interpreter's than anyone expects: she has to listen to languages that carry no words. A shaggy mammal rubbing itself along the fence asks for something quite different from a bird beating its wings behind glass. With the newborns she learns to bring up orphans on a bottle once the mother has gone; with wounded grown animals she does nothing but watch from a distance. Her patience belongs to someone tending a plot of ground, since a recovery cannot be hurried, only walked beside. The rest of the staff swear she can sense pain before the animal ever limps. She laughs at that and says she simply looks harder, and more often, and never in a rush.

units: the text weighs up a film about wildlife
the assessment falls into three aspects
the steadiness of the long takes is judged excellent
one sequence follows a bird of prey settling on a branch
the added music drowns the sound recorded on the spot
the commentary mixes up two different bodily states
one passage shows young that have just left the teat
that passage is held to be the best in the film
the crew never stated how long the watching sessions lasted
text: The wildlife film that went out last week deserves to be weighed on three separate counts rather than one. Visually it is faultless: the long takes hold rock steady, without a tremor, while the camera tracks a bird of prey coming down to settle on a branch. The sound is another matter altogether. Recording made on the spot keeps giving way to a wash of music that flattens the rustle of leaves and the scrape of feathers. Scientifically, the commentary blurs two states that are nothing alike, the animal sunk in winter sleep and the one that merely dozes off in spells, and the slip weakens an argument otherwise carefully built. What saves the picture is the long stretch given to the young the female has just weaned: no cutting tricks, only gestures handed on. A pity the crew never said how long it sat waiting in the field.

units: the letter is addressed to a woman living in the house next door
it concerns a ginger cat that moves from one plot to the other
the writer saw it at dusk hidden under a hedge
the animal was watching birds that had come to drink
the next day it settled on a window ledge
the writer first assumed it belonged to a tenant
the worn collar and the animal's thinness proved her wrong
she leaves it water but refuses to feed it
the animal walks badly on one hind leg
text: Dear neighbor, I am writing to you about the ginger cat that comes and goes between our two gardens. Late last week I caught sight of him at dusk, flattened under the hedge, keeping watch on the birds that come down to drink at the basin. The next morning he cleared the low wall and settled himself on the ledge of my window, quite at his ease. My first thought was that he belonged to the tenant at the far end, until I noticed the worn collar and how thin he has grown since. I have been leaving fresh water out for him, though I will not feed him, as I would rather he did not attach himself to my yard. Should you know who owns him, I would be grateful if you would pass the word along, since he favors one hind leg and walks poorly on it. I am happy to talk this over in person. With kind regards.

units: the wall of the egg grows thinner from the inside
the embryo draws off the calcium meant for its skeleton
a longer incubation yields a more finished young one
that young one moves about as soon as it leaves the shell
other species are born without feathers and without sight
this strategy shortens the time the female stays still over the clutch
it therefore lowers the risk of being spotted by a hunter
the adults must then feed young that cannot move
neither strategy is presented as the better one
text: What goes on inside an egg in the last hours before it opens? The shell grows thinner from within, because the embryo is drawing out the calcium that its skeleton needs. Why do some chicks arrive in down and others arrive bare? It turns on how long the sitting runs: the longer it lasts, the more finished the chick, ready to run about the moment it works its way free of the shell. And what does a species gain by hatching young that are naked and blind? It cuts short the stretch of time the female must hold still over the clutch, which lowers her chances of being picked out by a hunter. The bill comes later, when the parents have to feed a whole brood that cannot yet stir. So does one method win out over the other? No. Each answers what its surroundings demand, and neither would pay off elsewhere.

units: someone from the neighborhood tells of his troubles with keeping animals
his rabbits were digging under the fence and getting out
the runaways headed for the vegetable patch at the far end
the man had already sunk the wire mesh deeper
the animals were slipping through a gap he had not found
his daughter suggests laying a wide board flat against the fence
a digging animal starts its hole at the foot of the barrier
it gives up once it meets a hard surface
the family nailed boards down and then poured gravel over them
there has been no escape since
text: My neighbor stopped me at the gate to tell me the whole saga of his rabbits. They kept digging under the wire, he said, and heading straight for the vegetable patch at the far end. I asked whether he had tried sinking the mesh deeper. He had, he told me, and they still squeezed out through some gap he had never managed to find. His daughter was standing there listening, and she said, why not lay a wide board flat on the ground, right up against the fence. It struck me as sharp: an animal that digs goes at the base of whatever stands in its way, and once it meets something hard it quits. So they nailed the boards down and tipped gravel over the wood. Not one has got out since. He still laughs about it, because he was picturing a wall and she settled it with scrap lumber.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: two ways of taming animals existed at the same time
the first came about with no human intent
animals drew near the camps for the food scraps
they bred there alongside people
the second way rested on a choice made by keepers
the keepers held on to the calm animals and put aside the aggressive ones
this sorting produced bloodlines that do not exist in the wild
bones found in refuse heaps bear witness to the first process
pens and tethers bear witness to the second
the first process gave companions and the second gave herds
text: Two paths to taming ran side by side long before writing, and researchers still tell them apart. The first owed nothing to human intent. Animals drifted toward the camps for the scraps, put up with people at close range, and went on breeding right there, so the sorting happened with nobody meaning it. The second path was a matter of choice: keepers held on to the quietest beasts, weeded out the ones that turned on them, and within a handful of generations shaped bloodlines the wild had never produced. Bones dug out of old refuse heaps tell the first story. Pens and tethers tell the second. Specialists point out that one road delivered companions and the other delivered herds. The two overlap, of course, since an animal that came close by accident is one evening kept on purpose.

units: the text describes what a coat reveals
an even shade hides the animal in a stretch of sand or grass
a coat marked with spots mimics foliage shot through with light
those spots break up the animal's outline
tousled hair traps air against the skin
such hair keeps the body warm without weighing it down
swimmers wear a dense pelt that holds water off the skin
every coat also gives off a smell
a dog nosing a trunk picks up there that one of its own went by
the newly born wear a down that a breath will shift
text: A coat tells a story, and the eye has to work at it before the story comes clear. Start with plain color, which melts an animal into a wide stretch of sand or dry grass. Then the dappled coat, whose shadows mimic leaves punched through with light and break up the line of the back. Then the shaggy hair, tousled by wind, holding a layer of air against the skin and keeping the body warm with no weight to it. Then the sleek thick pelt of the swimmers, packed so tight that water slides straight across and never once reaches skin. Every coat carries a smell as well, and the smell travels: a dog nosing a trunk reads there that one of its own went by. Last of all comes the down of the newly born, so slight that a breath will shift it. Together they make up a language that nobody speaks aloud.

units: a team strung a fine net between two poles at the edge of a copse
the birds caught were measured and weighed and then let go
one bird marked the season before was taken again at the same spot
that second capture allowed a comparison of mass from one season to the next
the bird had lost a marked amount of weight
the loss fitted with a hard winter
the technician added two measurements to the protocol
she recorded wing length and the state of the plumage
the final report calls for longer watching of the site
the gear was left standing for the following season
text: At the start of the ringing season the team strung a fine net between two poles along the edge of a copse. Every bird that came in was measured, set on a field scale, and let go again in under a minute of handling. On the third evening a bird ringed the season before turned up in the same net, and that opened the way to comparing its mass from one season to the next. The figures showed a marked loss of weight, in keeping with a hard winter behind it. The technician changed the protocol on the spot: from then on she also took wing length and noted the state of the feathers, both of them signs of wear. By the close of the campaign the file held dozens of usable lines. The final report argues that the site deserves watching without a break, and the gear was left standing where it was.

units: a wall sheltered from the prevailing wind should be chosen
an exposed entrance lets rain in and chills the eggs
the support must be firm because a box that sways frightens the occupants
the entrance hole must stay narrow
a wide opening makes it easy for predators to get in
the box must hang beyond the reach of cats
no branch alongside should serve as a foothold
the inside should not be lined because the occupants bring their own material
a damp lining rots the brood
a clean-out at the end of the season clears parasites that would harm the next clutch
text: Before you put up a nesting box for small birds, pick a wall that lies out of the prevailing wind, since an exposed entrance takes in rain and chills the eggs inside. Screw the back plate to something solid and unmoving, because a box that sways unsettles the occupants and they will leave it at the first alarm. Cut the entrance hole narrow, as a wide one makes life far too easy for predators. Hang the whole thing beyond the reach of cats, shoulder height at the very least, and with no branch alongside that could serve as a foothold. Do not line the inside of it: the birds bring their own material, and a damp lining holds a moisture that rots the brood. Clean the cavity out once the season has ended, since the parasites piling up in the debris will spoil the clutch that follows.

units: walkers reported that the young ducks along a canal were disappearing
an association of naturalists looked into what was happening
the concrete slope kept the young from getting out of the water
the bread thrown in by passersby drew rodents
those rodents wrecked the nests
the local authority put in sloping wooden ramps that run below the surface
the young can climb these ramps without help
signs tell people that bread harms the birds
a later count found more surviving young
those in charge judge one season too little to draw a conclusion
text: Along the banks of a canal in town, walkers had been reporting for weeks that the duck broods were vanishing. An association of naturalists looked into it and came back with two causes. The concrete slope gave the ducklings no way out of the water, and rats drawn by the bread that passersby toss in were raiding the nests. The local authority began by fitting wooden ramps, set at a steep angle and running below the surface, which the young can climb up without help. Signs went up next, explaining that bread does the birds no good at all and feeds the rodents instead. A count taken when the warm season came round again turned up more surviving young than the year before. Those running the project are staying careful: one season proves nothing, and the watching will go on.
